html:
Barber pole — aperture problem
Motion overlay
real surface speed  ω·R = 0.60
apparent band speed = ω·R·tanθ = 0.28 (downward)
Guided demo
Drag to orbit and see the stripes wrap onto the far side — they are continuous helices, not sliding bars.
⚠ Figure failed to load

plan.contextChunk: This figure is a simple colored drawing of a barber pole standing upright on a white ground, annotated with two motion labels. The pole is a tall cylinder capped by an open ellipse, which gives it a three-dimensional read; its curved surface is wrapped by broad helical stripes alternating red, white, blue, and white, tilting downward from left to right and compressing toward the silhouette edges as they turn onto the far side. Above the cylinder, a nearly closed circular arrow drawn in a horizontal plane carries its arrowhead at the upper right, indicating spin about the vertical axis; the words "Real motion" sit above it. To the right, the words "Observed motion" head a short straight arrow pointing vertically downward. Putting a horizontal rotation arrow and a vertical perception arrow in one picture sets the physical direction against the perceived one. The drawing presents the barber-pole display as a case of the aperture problem: the stripes travel around the pole as it turns, yet seen only through the narrow window of the cylinder they register as moving downward.

elements: Tall vertical cylinder (barber pole) standing upright, open at the top
Elliptical rim at the top of the cylinder drawn as a black outline ring (open cap, white interior)
Elliptical bottom edge of the cylinder, black outline
Vertical black silhouette edges down the left and right of the cylinder
Helical stripe pattern wrapped on the curved surface: broad red band, white gap, broad blue band, white gap, repeating (~3 red + 3 blue bands visible on the front)
Perspective compression of the stripes toward the left and right silhouette edges as they turn onto the far side
Circular rotation arrow drawn in a horizontal plane above the cylinder, nearly closed, arrowhead at the upper right indicating spin about the vertical axis
Text label 'Real motion' above the circular arrow
Text label 'Observed motion' to the right of the cylinder
Short straight arrow below that label pointing vertically downward
Optional motion-tracer overlays: a dot riding a surface point around the cylinder, and a horizontal band marker riding a stripe edge downward

interactions.label: Spin the pole
interactions.teaches: Physical rotation about the vertical axis produces stripes that appear to march straight downward — the perceived direction is not the real one.

interactions.label: Motion overlay
interactions.teaches: Separating a tracked surface point (which circles horizontally) from a tracked stripe band (which slides vertically) shows the two incompatible readings of the same display.

interactions.label: Stripe angle from horizontal (deg)
interactions.teaches: Stripe orientation alone sets the perceived vertical speed: near-horizontal stripes appear almost static, steep stripes appear to race downward, because only the component normal to the stripe is measurable through the aperture.
Seeing the stripes wrap onto the hidden far side confirms they are continuous helices, not vertically translating bars.

demo_steps.title: The static pole
demo_steps.narration: A cylinder wrapped in red and blue helical stripes that rise to the right at about 25°. Nothing is moving yet.

demo_steps.title: Real motion: rotation
demo_steps.narration: Spin the pole about its vertical axis. The tracked surface dot travels horizontally around the cylinder — that is the true motion indicated by the circular arrow on top.

demo_steps.title: Observed motion: downward slide
demo_steps.narration: Switch the overlay to follow a stripe band instead. The same rotation now reads as bands sliding straight down, matching the 'Observed motion' arrow.

demo_steps.title: Both readings at once
demo_steps.narration: With both overlays on, the horizontal physical velocity and the vertical perceived velocity are visible simultaneously — the aperture problem in one picture.

demo_steps.title: Flatten the stripes
demo_steps.narration: Drop the stripe angle toward horizontal: the bands barely drift and the observed-motion arrow shrinks, even though the pole spins at the same rate.

demo_steps.title: Steepen the stripes
demo_steps.narration: Raise the angle toward vertical: the same rotation now drives a fast downward slide and a long observed-motion arrow.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Cylinder: radius 1.0, height 5.0 world units (screen aspect ≈ 1 wide : 2.5 tall), axis along +Y, centered on the origin so it spans y = -2.5 to +2.5. Open top: draw only the elliptical rim at y=+2.5 as a black torus/line ring, interior white (no cap fill shown from this slightly-above view). Bottom rim at y=-2.5 also a black ellipse. Camera slightly above eye level (elev ≈ 12°) so the top rim reads as an ellipse about 0.28 as tall as it is wide; the bottom rim shows only a shallow curve. Stripes: helical bands painted on the curved surface, pattern period along the axis such that ~6 colored bands (3 red, 3 blue) are visible on the front face; band angular width ≈ 0.22 of the period in the stripe-normal direction, separated by equal white gaps (order red, white, blue, white). Stripes rise to the RIGHT (left end lower, right end higher) at the slider angle, default 25° above horizontal on the unrolled surface — generate as texture: color = f(u*tan? ) use phase = (v/H)*cos(theta) - (u/2π)*sin(theta)... simplest: phase = (y - k*x_angle) where k = cot(angle); tile 4 stripe periods over the height at 25°. Rotation: clockwise seen from above (front surface moves to screen-RIGHT), ω ≈ 0.6 rad/s; combined with right-rising stripes this yields apparent DOWNWARD band motion at speed v_y = ω·R / tan(theta). Colors: red #EE0000 / pure #FF0000, blue #0000FF, white #FFFFFF, outlines and text black #000000 with ~4px strokes. 'Real motion' text sits top-left above the pole; the rotation arrow is a horizontal ellipse (semi-axes 1.2 x 0.35) centered on the axis at y ≈ +3.6, drawn as a nearly closed arc with a ~30° gap, its solid triangular arrowhead at the upper-right of the ellipse pointing left/counterclockwise-in-screen along the far arc. 'Observed motion' text is to the right of the cylinder at roughly mid-height (x ≈ +2.6, y ≈ +0.6), with a straight downward arrow directly beneath it from y ≈ +0.1 to y ≈ -1.0, arrowhead at the bottom; its length scales with the computed apparent vertical speed.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the stripe pattern as a procedural shader or CanvasTexture on an open-ended THREE.CylinderGeometry (openEnded: true, radialSegments 96, DoubleSide) so the helix angle can be changed live from the slider without rebuilding geometry; animate rotation by advancing the texture's helical phase or rotating the mesh about Y — rotating the mesh is preferred so the tracked surface dot stays glued to a real point. Add the top rim as a separate torus or thick LineLoop and a subtle white interior disk slightly below the rim to suggest the hollow open top. Silhouette outlines: render a slightly scaled back-face black shell or use an outline pass so the left/right edges read as bold black lines like the source. The tracked surface dot is a small black sphere parented to the cylinder at radius 1.01; the observed-band marker is a thin horizontal ring at constant radius whose y decreases at v_y = ω·R/tan(theta), wrapping when it leaves the bottom. Labels ('Real motion', 'Observed motion') and the two arrows as HTML/CSS2D overlays or sprites in a serif font, kept screen-aligned and non-rotating during orbit. Clamp theta away from 0 to avoid division blow-up; at very small angles cap the arrow length and apparent speed.

### Representation of Optical Flow

discrepancies: Stripe period is too fine: the source shows roughly 4 wide red and 4 wide blue bands across the pole, while the generated pole shows ~7-8 of each, so the bands read as thin ribbons rather than the broad barber-pole helices.

The 'Real motion' rotation arrow is rendered nearly edge-on (camera elevation 12°), so it collapses into a horizontal black line with a blob instead of the clear elliptical loop with a distinct arrowhead shown in the source.
The top ellipse of the cylinder is much thinner than in the source, which shows a pronounced open white top ellipse — the viewpoint is flatter than the source's slightly-raised view.

Extra elements not in the source (black tracked-point sphere, grey path ring, green band ring, small overlay text labels) sit on top of the pole; the 'tracked surface point' caption overlaps the striped surface and is hard to read against red/blue.
Overall composition places the pole left of centre with the observed-motion arrow much closer in; the source has a tighter, more symmetric layout with the arrow well clear of the pole.
evaluation.notes: A genuinely 3D, shader-striped barber pole with correct physics (v = ωR·tanθ) and a rich, functional control set; main weaknesses are too-fine stripe spacing, a rotation arrow flattened to a line by the low camera elevation, and small overlay labels that clutter the pole surface.
action_items: Increase the stripe period (larger W) so roughly 4 red and 4 blue bands span the pole height, matching the source's broad helices.

Raise the camera elevation to ~18-22° (or tilt/enlarge the rotation-arrow arc) so the 'Real motion' loop reads as a clear ellipse with a visible arrowhead, and the open top ellipse is as prominent as in the source.
Move the 'tracked surface point' and 'tracked stripe band' captions off the striped surface (offset outward with a light background) and increase their font size for legibility.
Verify the helix handedness so the stripes ascend to the right on the front face exactly as in the source, and re-centre the pole in the viewport with the observed-motion arrow further to the right.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct (no plan-level action items); all issues are concrete rendering fixes like stripe period, camera elevation, label placement, and layout.

plan.contextChunk: This figure is a simple colored drawing of a barber pole standing upright on a white ground, annotated with two motion labels. The pole is a tall cylinder capped by an open ellipse, which gives it a three-dimensional read; its curved surface is wrapped by broad helical stripes alternating red, white, blue, and white, tilting downward from left to right and compressing toward the silhouette edges as they turn onto the far side. Above the cylinder, a nearly closed circular arrow drawn in a horizontal plane carries its arrowhead at the upper right, indicating spin about the vertical axis; the words "Real motion" sit above it. To the right, the words "Observed motion" head a short straight arrow pointing vertically downward. Putting a horizontal rotation arrow and a vertical perception arrow in one picture sets the physical direction against the perceived one. The drawing presents the barber-pole display as a case of the aperture problem: the stripes travel around the pole as it turns, yet seen only through the narrow window of the cylinder they register as moving downward.

elements: Tall vertical cylinder (barber pole) standing upright, open at the top
Elliptical rim at the top of the cylinder drawn as a black outline ring (open cap, white interior)
Elliptical bottom edge of the cylinder, black outline
Vertical black silhouette edges down the left and right of the cylinder
Helical stripe pattern wrapped on the curved surface: broad red band, white gap, broad blue band, white gap, repeating (~3 red + 3 blue bands visible on the front)
Perspective compression of the stripes toward the left and right silhouette edges as they turn onto the far side
Circular rotation arrow drawn in a horizontal plane above the cylinder, nearly closed, arrowhead at the upper right indicating spin about the vertical axis
Text label 'Real motion' above the circular arrow
Text label 'Observed motion' to the right of the cylinder
Short straight arrow below that label pointing vertically downward
Optional motion-tracer overlays: a dot riding a surface point around the cylinder, and a horizontal band marker riding a stripe edge downward

interactions.label: Spin the pole
interactions.teaches: Physical rotation about the vertical axis produces stripes that appear to march straight downward — the perceived direction is not the real one.

interactions.label: Motion overlay
interactions.teaches: Separating a tracked surface point (which circles horizontally) from a tracked stripe band (which slides vertically) shows the two incompatible readings of the same display.

interactions.label: Stripe angle from horizontal (deg)
interactions.teaches: Stripe orientation alone sets the perceived vertical speed: near-horizontal stripes appear almost static, steep stripes appear to race downward, because only the component normal to the stripe is measurable through the aperture.
Seeing the stripes wrap onto the hidden far side confirms they are continuous helices, not vertically translating bars.

demo_steps.title: The static pole
demo_steps.narration: A cylinder wrapped in red and blue helical stripes that rise to the right at about 25°. Nothing is moving yet.

demo_steps.title: Real motion: rotation
demo_steps.narration: Spin the pole about its vertical axis. The tracked surface dot travels horizontally around the cylinder — that is the true motion indicated by the circular arrow on top.

demo_steps.title: Observed motion: downward slide
demo_steps.narration: Switch the overlay to follow a stripe band instead. The same rotation now reads as bands sliding straight down, matching the 'Observed motion' arrow.

demo_steps.title: Both readings at once
demo_steps.narration: With both overlays on, the horizontal physical velocity and the vertical perceived velocity are visible simultaneously — the aperture problem in one picture.

demo_steps.title: Flatten the stripes
demo_steps.narration: Drop the stripe angle toward horizontal: the bands barely drift and the observed-motion arrow shrinks, even though the pole spins at the same rate.

demo_steps.title: Steepen the stripes
demo_steps.narration: Raise the angle toward vertical: the same rotation now drives a fast downward slide and a long observed-motion arrow.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Cylinder: radius 1.0, height 5.0 world units (screen aspect ≈ 1 wide : 2.5 tall), axis along +Y, centered on the origin so it spans y = -2.5 to +2.5. Open top: draw only the elliptical rim at y=+2.5 as a black torus/line ring, interior white (no cap fill shown from this slightly-above view). Bottom rim at y=-2.5 also a black ellipse. Camera slightly above eye level (elev ≈ 12°) so the top rim reads as an ellipse about 0.28 as tall as it is wide; the bottom rim shows only a shallow curve. Stripes: helical bands painted on the curved surface, pattern period along the axis such that ~6 colored bands (3 red, 3 blue) are visible on the front face; band angular width ≈ 0.22 of the period in the stripe-normal direction, separated by equal white gaps (order red, white, blue, white). Stripes rise to the RIGHT (left end lower, right end higher) at the slider angle, default 25° above horizontal on the unrolled surface — generate as texture: color = f(u*tan? ) use phase = (v/H)*cos(theta) - (u/2π)*sin(theta)... simplest: phase = (y - k*x_angle) where k = cot(angle); tile 4 stripe periods over the height at 25°. Rotation: clockwise seen from above (front surface moves to screen-RIGHT), ω ≈ 0.6 rad/s; combined with right-rising stripes this yields apparent DOWNWARD band motion at speed v_y = ω·R / tan(theta). Colors: red #EE0000 / pure #FF0000, blue #0000FF, white #FFFFFF, outlines and text black #000000 with ~4px strokes. 'Real motion' text sits top-left above the pole; the rotation arrow is a horizontal ellipse (semi-axes 1.2 x 0.35) centered on the axis at y ≈ +3.6, drawn as a nearly closed arc with a ~30° gap, its solid triangular arrowhead at the upper-right of the ellipse pointing left/counterclockwise-in-screen along the far arc. 'Observed motion' text is to the right of the cylinder at roughly mid-height (x ≈ +2.6, y ≈ +0.6), with a straight downward arrow directly beneath it from y ≈ +0.1 to y ≈ -1.0, arrowhead at the bottom; its length scales with the computed apparent vertical speed.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the stripe pattern as a procedural shader or CanvasTexture on an open-ended THREE.CylinderGeometry (openEnded: true, radialSegments 96, DoubleSide) so the helix angle can be changed live from the slider without rebuilding geometry; animate rotation by advancing the texture's helical phase or rotating the mesh about Y — rotating the mesh is preferred so the tracked surface dot stays glued to a real point. Add the top rim as a separate torus or thick LineLoop and a subtle white interior disk slightly below the rim to suggest the hollow open top. Silhouette outlines: render a slightly scaled back-face black shell or use an outline pass so the left/right edges read as bold black lines like the source. The tracked surface dot is a small black sphere parented to the cylinder at radius 1.01; the observed-band marker is a thin horizontal ring at constant radius whose y decreases at v_y = ω·R/tan(theta), wrapping when it leaves the bottom. Labels ('Real motion', 'Observed motion') and the two arrows as HTML/CSS2D overlays or sprites in a serif font, kept screen-aligned and non-rotating during orbit. Clamp theta away from 0 to avoid division blow-up; at very small angles cap the arrow length and apparent speed.
